title: Annapurna treks compared: which one fits your days
meta_description: Poon Hill, Mardi Himal, Annapurna Base Camp, Khopra or the Circuit? Days, heights, grades and seasons compared, from people who walk them every year.
summary: With three to five days, walk Poon Hill and Ghandruk. With a week, Mardi Himal. With ten to twelve days, Annapurna Base Camp. With two to three weeks and a head for altitude, the Annapurna Circuit over Thorong La. For quiet, Khopra ridge, Panchase or the Royal Trek. The table below sets them side by side.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Every trek in the Annapurnas starts from Pokhara or close to it, and every one of them gives you big mountains. The difference is time, height and how many other people you will share the trail with. The Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal's largest protected area at about 7,600 square km, holds the most walked trails in the country, but also ridges where you can go a whole day without meeting another trekker.

Ask yourself three questions. How many walking days do you have, not counting flights and a spare day? How high do you want to sleep: below 3,000 m, where altitude sickness is rare, or above 4,000 m, where it is a real factor? And do you want villages and people along the way, or open ridges and silence? The answers usually choose the trek for you.

Season matters as much as the trek. October and November are the clearest months on every route. March and April bring rhododendron forests in flower, warmer nights and more afternoon cloud. December to February suits the low treks, while snow can close Thorong La and make the upper ABC trail risky. From June to September the monsoon brings leeches, cloud and slippery stone steps, although the rain-shadow side of the Circuit around Manang and Muktinath stays fairly dry.

sections.heading: The main treks side by side
paras: Nights below are counted from Pokhara and back, walking at a comfortable pace with a licensed guide. Fit trekkers can shave a day or two from most of them, but we would not cut acclimatisation days on the higher routes.

Add a night in Kathmandu at each end if you are flying in from abroad, and one spare day for weather on the longer treks. Domestic flights to Pokhara and Jomsom are often delayed by cloud, and a landslide on a jeep road can cost half a day in the monsoon months. A trek planned without slack is the one most likely to go wrong.

sections.heading: Poon Hill and Ghandruk: the classic loop
paras: This is the trek most people mean when they say they did a short trek in Nepal. You climb the stone staircase from Tikhedhunga to Ulleri, walk through rhododendron forest to Ghorepani at 2,860 m, and climb Poon Hill at dawn for a line of peaks from Dhaulagiri I to Annapurna II. The return through Tadapani and the Gurung village of Ghandruk means no backtracking.

It is busy in October, November, March and April, with a few hundred people on the summit some mornings. The lodges are good, the trail is easy to follow and the highest night is low enough that altitude is rarely a problem. If you only have four or five days in the region, choose this.

The walk also shows two peoples. Ulleri and Ghorepani are Magar villages, and Poon Hill is named after the Pun clan of Magars who live around it. Ghandruk is Gurung, with a museum of everyday objects and many families with Gurkha service. A guide who grew up in the area turns the trek from a view into a story.

sections.heading: Mardi Himal: the ridge walk
paras: Mardi Himal follows a single grass ridge from Australian Camp through cloud forest to High Camp at about 3,580 m, then on a dawn walk to an upper viewpoint at about 4,200 m and, for some, to base camp at about 4,500 m. Machhapuchhre's west face is in front of you for two days. Lodges are small and few, especially at High Camp, so book early in season.

It has become popular in the last decade but is still less crowded than ABC. The walk up to the viewpoint is long and exposed to wind, and above 4,000 m it is high enough for headaches. In five or six nights it gives a stronger high-mountain feeling than any other short trek in the region.

sections.heading: Annapurna Base Camp: inside the sanctuary
paras: ABC is the trek for those who want to stand inside a ring of peaks. You walk through Gurung villages to Chhomrong, then up the Modi Khola gorge through bamboo and rhododendron to Machhapuchhre Base Camp at 3,700 m and Annapurna Base Camp at 4,130 m. Annapurna I, the first 8,000 m peak climbed, in 1950, stands to the north, with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre around you.

Allow eight to ten nights from Pokhara. The steps around Chhomrong are hard, and the sections above Deurali cross old avalanche paths that can close briefly after heavy snow in late winter and spring. Above Chhomrong, by long custom, lodges serve no meat. It is the best value big-mountain trek in Nepal.

The trek can be joined to Poon Hill by crossing from Ghorepani through Tadapani to Chhomrong, which adds two or three days and gives your body nights near 2,800 m before the climb into the sanctuary. On the way down, the natural hot springs at Jhinu Danda, a short walk below the lodges, are the best reward on any Annapurna trail.

sections.heading: The Annapurna Circuit: the long way round
paras: The Circuit goes all the way round the Annapurna massif: up the Marsyangdi valley through Hindu and Gurung villages, into the Tibetan Buddhist valley of Manang, over Thorong La at 5,416 m, and down to Muktinath and the Kali Gandaki. No other trek in Nepal shows so many cultures and landscapes in one walk.

Roads now reach Manang and Muktinath, which changed the trek. Walkers who use the side trails, the high route via Ghyaru and Ngawal, and a flight out of Jomsom still get a great trek. You need at least two nights at Manang for acclimatisation and a reserve day for the pass, which can close after snow from December to March.

The rewards are worth the planning. Manang's stone villages, the cliffside monastery at Praken, the pilgrims at Muktinath's 108 water spouts and the mud-brick lanes of Kagbeni are among the most memorable places in Nepal. This is the trek for walkers who have done a shorter route and want something bigger, and who can give it at least two weeks.

sections.heading: The quieter choices
paras: If crowds put you off, three routes are worth a look. Khopra ridge leaves the Poon Hill trail at Ghorepani and climbs through forest to a community lodge at 3,660 m facing Dhaulagiri I across the Kali Gandaki gorge; the lodges here bring income to villages in Myagdi. Panchase, the forested hill south-west of Pokhara, lies outside the conservation area and gives a sunrise view from 2,517 m after two easy days. The Royal Trek, named after the Prince of Wales's walk in 1980, stays below 2,000 m in villages above Begnas Lake.
These are simpler trips, with homestays and small lodges rather than big teahouses. They suit travellers who care more about people and quiet than about a famous name.

Facilities are basic on all three. Expect shared toilets, hot water in a bucket in some homes and simple meals of dal bhat, greens and pickles. In return you sit by a family hearth rather than in a lodge dining room, and the money you spend goes straight to the village. Each of these routes can be walked in three to eight nights from Pokhara.

sections.heading: How we would choose
paras: If you are still undecided, these rules of thumb rarely steer anyone wrong.
list: Under a week and first time in Nepal: Poon Hill and Ghandruk.
A week, good fitness, want to feel high: Mardi Himal.
Ten days or more and one big goal: Annapurna Base Camp.
Two to three weeks, previous trekking, and keen on culture: the Annapurna Circuit.
Children under ten or older walkers: Dhampus and Australian Camp, or the Royal Trek.
December to February: stay below 3,000 m, where Poon Hill, Panchase and the Royal Trek are clear and safe.

faqs.q: Which Annapurna trek is best for beginners?
faqs.a: Poon Hill and Ghandruk is the best first trek: four or five nights from Pokhara, a highest night of 2,860 m, good lodges and a famous sunrise view from 3,210 m. For something easier still, Dhampus and Australian Camp takes two or three nights below 2,100 m. Both need only reasonable fitness and some training on stairs.

faqs.q: Is Mardi Himal harder than Poon Hill?
faqs.a: Yes. Mardi Himal goes higher, to around 4,200 to 4,500 m at the viewpoint and base camp, with a long, exposed summit day and fewer lodges. Poon Hill tops out at 3,210 m with shorter days. Mardi suits fit walkers with some hill experience; Poon Hill suits almost anyone who can climb stairs for several hours.

faqs.q: Which is better, ABC or the Annapurna Circuit?
faqs.a: They are different trips. ABC is shorter, eight to ten nights from Pokhara, and ends in a ring of peaks at 4,130 m. The Circuit takes two to three weeks, crosses a 5,416 m pass and passes through many cultures. Choose ABC for a focused mountain trek; choose the Circuit for a long journey with more variety.

faqs.q: Which Annapurna trek has the fewest crowds?
faqs.a: Khopra ridge, Panchase and the Royal Trek see far fewer trekkers than Poon Hill or ABC. Mardi Himal is busier than it was but quieter than ABC. On the Circuit, the high route through Ghyaru and Ngawal and the NATT trails away from the road are much quieter than the main path.

faqs.q: What is the shortest Annapurna trek with good mountain views?
faqs.a: Australian Camp, two hours' walk from the road at Kande, gives a full view of Machhapuchhre and the Annapurnas, and can be done in one or two nights from Pokhara. For a bigger panorama, Poon Hill needs three or four nights. Sarangkot, above Pokhara, gives a similar view by car but without the trek.

faqs.q: Do all Annapurna treks need a guide?
faqs.a: Under rules in force since April 2023, foreign trekkers in the Annapurna Conservation Area must hire a licensed guide through a registered agency. This covers Poon Hill, ABC, Mardi Himal, Khopra and the Circuit. Panchase and much of the Royal Trek lie outside the conservation area. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which Annapurna trek is best in winter?
faqs.a: From December to February, choose a lower trek: Poon Hill, Ghandruk, Panchase, Dhampus and Australian Camp, or the Royal Trek. Skies are very clear and days mild, though nights are cold. ABC is possible with care but can have avalanche risk above Deurali, and Thorong La on the Circuit is often closed by snow.

faqs.q: Can I combine two Annapurna treks?
faqs.a: Yes. The most common combination is Poon Hill with ABC, crossing from Ghorepani via Tadapani to Chhomrong, which takes about twelve nights from Pokhara and helps acclimatisation. Khopra can also link to ABC, and Australian Camp is the natural start of the Mardi Himal trail.

faqs.q: Which trek has the best view of Machhapuchhre?
faqs.a: Mardi Himal gives the closest view, with the west face filling the sky from High Camp and the viewpoint above it. Machhapuchhre Base Camp on the ABC trek shows the peak from the sanctuary side. For an easy view, Australian Camp and Tadapani both face the mountain directly.
